How to get rid of springtails, moisture first, in order: fix leaks and drips, ventilate the bathroom, run a dehumidifier, let houseplant soil dry between waterings, pull mulch and leaf litter back from the foundation, seal gaps, vacuum the ones indoors (Colorado State, UMN); insecticides only at the sources' strength (Colorado State advises avoiding them indoors where possible; UMN says there are no pesticides for springtails in houseplants), never a home-remedy spray. Quick-ID table: the springtail and its look-alikes (flea, booklouse, mite, fungus gnat larva in soil), one row each: size, color, how it moves, where you find it, bites or not. pages.scope: Camel crickets for US and Canadian readers, identification first: a humpbacked, wingless cricket, light tan to dark brown, with antennae much longer than its body and large hind legs, that never chirps (no sound-making organs, per Clemson HGIC; chirping indoors points to field crickets, per NC State) and jumps a surprisingly long way (MDC); sizes only from sources (Clemson: 1/2 to 1 1/2 inches; MDC: body up to about 1 inch). The "jumps at you" reputation only as a source puts it: NC State, Clemson and MDC do not say they jump toward people, and it is never an attack. Which ones get into homes: the greenhouse camel cricket (Tachycines asynamorus, also written Diestrammena asynamora), the most common camel cricket in eastern US homes (Epps et al. 2014, PeerJ; NC State), and the native camel or cave crickets (Ceuthophilus); nymphs look like small adults (NC State). Then the "spider cricket" question, spider or cricket (six legs and long antennae against a spider's eight legs and none), with look-alike cards: house and field cricket (crickets-in-house, once live), cellar spider (/blog/house-spiders), wolf spider (/blog/wolf-spiders), house centipede (/blog/house-centipedes). Where they live and why they come in: damp basements, crawl spaces, garages and laundry rooms; outdoors under stones, logs, firewood, mulch and ivy; large numbers point to a moisture problem (MDC); whether they breed indoors, where sources differ (MDC and Iowa State: unlikely unless it stays dark and damp; Cornell's Nassau County office: they can). Bites and harm at the sources' strength: none of the sources read reports a bite (MDC and Kentucky call them harmless); damage only as Clemson (fine fabrics and houseplants when numerous) and NC State (stored garments and linens after a long infestation; dark fecal smears on joists) put it. A control section, since this page owns "how to get rid of camel crickets": dry the space, seal and weather-strip, pull mulch, firewood and stored boxes back from walls, sticky traps in corners and behind appliances, vacuum (NC State, Clemson); insecticides only as those sources put them (perimeter first, baits in crawl spaces, a product labeled for the site; the label is the law), no product names. One line each, linked once live: chirping crickets (crickets-in-house) and the unrelated desert camel spider (camel-spiders); the western Jerusalem cricket is another family (UC IPM), one line at most. Sources: NC State Extension's Camel Crickets (revised 2023), Clemson HGIC, University of Maryland Extension, University of Kentucky, MDC, Iowa State, Epps et al. 2014.
